title: Secure Automation and Operational Safety knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Secure Automation and Operational Safety”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Dry-run support” under lesson 137, “Secure Automation and Operational Safety”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Secure Automation and Operational Safety”?
options: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
questions.answer_key: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
questions.explanation: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Secure Automation and Operational Safety”?
options: Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Validate the exact target, use a preview for side effects, and verify the result before reporting success.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
questions.answer_key: Validate the exact target, use a preview for side effects, and verify the result before reporting success.
questions.explanation: Validate the exact target, use a preview for side effects, and verify the result before reporting success. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
